## The question

[Simple Geometric Patterns](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5145283/simple-geometric-patterns), asked by [Reuben](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/700617/reuben) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2026-07-28; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> So I am having a hard time understanding exactly what defines a pattern. I am not sure if a pattern needs to transform from one motif to the next or simply within a motif.
>
> **Example1**: this is a translation pattern
>
> [![enter image description here][q-1]][q-1]
>
> Each arrow is translated onto the next arrows position.
>
> **Example2**: This is a reflection pattern
>
> [![enter image description here][q-2]][q-2]
>
> Each arrow is reflected horizontally onto the next arrows position
>
> **Example3**: This is a glide reflection pattern (or a rotationpattern)
>
> [![enter image description here][q-3]][q-3]
>
> **Question**: will it be accurate to simply say that example3 is a reflection pattern due to the fact the arrows do reflect vertically? Or do the "rules" require us to land on the next "position"? From what I understand, if example 1 is a translation pattern and not a "nothing pattern", then it seems to follow that we need to include the transformation between motifs. By this I would assume that if someone was asked to draw a refelction pattern as presented Example3 it would be correct
>
>
>
>   [q-1]: TMrH1mNJ.png
>   [q-2]: 2K61wQM6.png
>   [q-3]: M6CJYu8p.png
:::

The term I am familiar with for these patterns is [*frieze*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frieze_group), and they are classified by their symmetries. Once you identify all the symmetries, you'll find that there are relations between them. Meaning that some of the symmetries are redundant.

All of the patterns have translational symmetry, and the symmetries you found. But there are some that you missed.

* Pattern 1 also has a vertical reflection symmetry (parallel to the arrow through its point). The symmetry group is called p1m1. 

* Pattern 2 has a horizontal reflection, a vertical reflection, and a 180° rotation (around the point midway between the tips of the arrows). The two reflections generate the rotation. Translation and one of the reflections generate a glide reflection. The symmetry group is called p2mm.

* Pattern 3 has a vertical reflection, a 180° rotation, and a glide reflection. The symmetry group is called p2mg.
